title: Simultaneous Bands for External-Instrument Impulse Responses over Growing Horizons
banked_reason: D0.5.G tier=subfield < floor=field, paper_score_ceiling 6.9 < 7.4, salvageable=false; sound growing-horizon achievability lacks necessity or minimax boundary under restrictive primitives.
gap_reasons: The delivered result is an achievability theorem for simultaneous growing-horizon bands over a restrictive exact-sparse, sub-Gaussian, geometrically mixing, strong-IV class; it proves neither a necessary horizon boundary nor a minimax result.

The projected paper score is constrained by the narrow primitives, the absence of simulation or empirical evidence showing finite-sample usefulness, and literature positioning that asserts novelty of the assembled regime without a theorem-level comparison demonstrating which existing growing-path arguments fail.

Given the declared estimand functional and M != 0 from ass:strong-first-stage, E[z_t e_{t,h}] = E[z_t(Y_{t+h}-m_{Y,h}(U_t))]-theta_h M = 0 identically; this is not an additional model restriction and should be derived rather than maintained as A_IV.

The positioning omits Montiel Olea--Plagborg-Møller (2019), the established simultaneous-SVAR-band result with an external-instrument application; add it and state precisely why its fixed-dimensional SVAR/sup-t setting does not deliver this learned-score, growing-horizon theorem.
proof_attempt_summary: Discovery built a theorem graph for feasible simultaneous external-IV response bands at every fixed horizon exponent below 1/2, with a separate alignment-localized covariance estimator attaining a root-T polylogarithmic rate. Cited Gaussian and coupling results were attested against source text, and D0.5 judged the mathematics sound but the achieved novelty subfield under the standing field floor. A field-tier successor would need a distinct necessity/minimax result or a substantial model-class extension; the redundant IV assumption and omitted comparator remain recorded as tier-neutral cleanup.
tldr: For every fixed \(0<\alpha<1/2\), the stationary sparse external-instrument family admits uniform Gaussian maximum approximation and feasible unconditional \(95\%\) simultaneous bands with half-width \(O_P(\sqrt{\log H_{T,\alpha}/T})\), allowing singular cross-horizon correlation. The original log-corrected Bartlett module retains error \(O_P[T^{-(1-2\alpha)/4}\{\log(2d_{T,\alpha})\}^{1/4}]\). A distinct alignment-localized covariance module, retaining logarithmic neighborhoods of the four score-endpoint alignments and then using a measurable positive-semidefinite selector, sharpens its own covariance error to \(O_P(T^{-1/2}\log^{3/2}T)\). At \(\alpha_0=1/12\), these two module-specific rates are respectively \(T^{-5/24}(\log T)^{1/4}\) and \(T^{-1/2}\log^{3/2}T\). No minimax or necessity claim is made.
gap: The closest same-target paper stops at fixed-horizon Gaussian and HAC inference. Gonçalves, Herrera, Kilian, Pesavento, and Holban (2026), Introduction lines 50--57, study a predetermined observed structural shock using a doubly robust density-ratio moment with neighbors-left-out cross-fitting, and Section 5, Theorem 5.1, lines 244--250 proves per-horizon scalar asymptotic normality. Existing long-horizon LP theory omits the learned external-IV score, while fixed-dimensional SVAR-IV weak-instrument inference and quasi-Bayesian joint LP--IV bands address different regimes.
fill: At \(\alpha_0=1/12\), the project derives one feasible learned external-IV estimator's uniform influence expansion, oracle Gaussian maximum law, full cross-horizon Bartlett covariance rate, vanishing fallback probability, and unconditional simultaneous coverage from explicitly indexed primitive conditions. These deliverables are distinct from the per-horizon scalar asymptotic normality proved by Gonçalves et al. for a predetermined observed structural shock with a doubly robust density-ratio moment and neighbors-left-out cross-fitting. Coefficient norm bounds and response boundedness are derived rather than imposed, and a direct Gaussian finite-filter membership lemma certifies nonvacuity.
